utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, accused Popovic is temporarily absent from the courtroom, being attended to for a medical problem that he has encountered. We are -- otherwise we are full house. We can proceed. A few things that we would like to raise with you. One is there is a motion from the Prosecution for the issue of a subpoena. You have been served with a copy, I suppose. Yes. Since this is pretty urgent, we are talking of someone who should be here very latest next week, early next week. Are there any objections? I hear none. The motion is granted, but since you will need a written copy, it is being attended to, I will have a look at it and then we will hand down the decision during the day. There is another motion from the Prosecution filed on the 12th of January to convert three viva voce witnesses to Rule 92 ter witnesses, we're talking about 78, 79 and 80, the first of whom will be the next one after we're finished with this witness today. Are there any objections from the Defence teams to have these witnesses testify as Rule 92 ter? I hear none. So that motion is granted, and that will not be followed by a written. Last Friday, Madam Fauveau raised the issue as to whether the time limits that we communicated to you during the day would apply to the next witness being the cryptographic witness. Our decision is that we will not apply the time limits in any rigid way, however we will see how, because of course I mean we don't have an idea what this person is going to testify upon, and we'll deal with it as we go along. What we will certainly do is in conformity with our communication to you, we will control both the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination in case there are questions dealing with issues that we don't think we ought to hear any more about. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If it is of assistance to you and my learned friends, Mr. Nicholls has advised that me he intends to try to comply to the half-hour limit with witness number 78. It may require more than that, but just to give you an idea of the time we anticipate with him, it will be about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have communicated our decision, in other words, that you remain within the parameters that we mentioned, et cetera, the 30- minute limit applicable to you and the 20 minutes applicable to the various Defence teams can be extended depending on circumstances, if there is a just cause. All right. Can we bring in the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And guards, please, any time Mr. Popovic can return to the courtroom, you may escort him straight away, you don't need to inform us beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence, and our rules require that before you do so you enter a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be testifying the truth. The text is going to be handed to you now. Please read that, read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I understand. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have probably been informed already that we granted you some protective measures, namely facial distortion and also the use of a pseudonym instead of your name. I trust this has been explained to you and it is satisfactory to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have been informed about the protective measures and I am satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You will first be examined in chief by Mr. Thayer, to be followed by cross-examination by some of the Defence teams. Go ahead, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon again, learned friends, all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With the court usher's assistance, I will be handed to you a document, and without reading it aloud, just read it to yourself, please. Would you just confirm that your name appears next to the number PW-123?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that is --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, my name is on the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that is PO2351, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, before I begin asking you just a few questions about your prior testimony, I wanted to ask you one biographical questions and fill in a couple of details about your military service. Mr. President, may we briefly enter private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn your attention to your testimony in the Blagojevic case. Was that entire testimony read to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, I did read the entire statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, in fact, the transcript was read to you by one of our language assistants; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes. I was read and the -- to, and the transcript was translated to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you bring any inaccuracies to my attention after having that transcript read to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: From what I understood, in one section it was translated as if somebody was standing above me and telling me where I would be putting the full stops. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll talk about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. For the record, the Trial Chamber notes that Mr. Popovic has come -- has entered into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, should you have any problems during the sitting that requires our attention during the sitting, please let us know straight away. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, we'll talk about the transcript and any inaccuracies in just a moment. Let me get through a couple of items first. Can you attest before the Trial Chamber that other than any of the inaccuracies that we will talk about shortly, the transcript which was read to you accurately reflects your testimony in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: It's my testimony for the most part. That part that wasn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that other than that part the transcript which was read to you was accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, the rest of it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the transcript, does it reflect what you would say if actually questioned as reflected in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Well, it would be difficult to repeat it word for word. I know the procedure that I put into practice, but I don't know if I would be able to use the same words to describe what I was doing. That is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But the substance of the testimony that is contained in that transcript is what you would testify to if you were actually questioned upon that? Is that fair to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, that could be so. You could say it like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to read to you a summary of your Blagojevic testimony, after which we'll talk about a couple of those inaccuracies. The witness is a Bosniak Muslim. He completed secondary school and was a member of a radio amateur club, with which he competed in monthly radio amateur competitions. He obtained a C grade certificate in 1984. He performed his mandatory JNA service in 1988 and 1989 in a signals company, where for the second six months of his service he commanded a squad in charge of two APCs carrying the brigade's communications equipment. Following his JNA service, he remained a member of the radio amateur, club and continued to take part in monthly competitions. In July of 1992, he joined the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and served in the electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare unit. He obtained a B category certificate in 1993. In the winter of 1993, he was transferred to the northern location. He was then transferred to the southern location in May 1994. He had previously been to the southern location, because some of the radio amateur competitions were held there, although not at the military facilities. In July 1995, he was still stationed at the southern location. In his testimony, he described the shift structure, composition and duration. He also described the equipment they used and the procedures they followed to intercept and transcribe VRS conversations. He identified his handwritten transcription of a 14 July 1995 conversation at 9.05 a.m. in an original notebook and a photocopy of it. His transcription indicates that the participants are a duty officer and General Zivanovic. They were familiar with Zivanovic's voice and the phone he was using, which was very peculiar. He was not sure if it was Zivanovic's voice or his phone which was the basis for this particular identification. He then recognised a typed printout of this transcribed conversation. He also identified his handwritten transcription of a 14 July 1995 conversation at 9.35 a.m. from the same original notebook and a photocopy of it. He then recognised a typed printout of this transcribed conversation. Finally, he identified his handwriting in a number of original notebooks from the southern location. Another member of the company back in command was in charge of giving the notebook numbers and the date when the notebook was given out. This registration date did not necessarily coincide with the first date on which the notebook was used to transcribe intercepts. And that concludes the summary. Sir, did that -- was that summary accurate to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, if we may just go into private session briefly because I will be citing the actual Blagojevic transcript by page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are already in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you just a couple of questions about one of the intercepts only, and that's the one located at tab 1 of the packet. And with the -- madam usher's assistance, I would just ask that a copy of the packet be handed to the witness, just as a back-up, please. And in the meantime, may we have PO2352B put on e-court, please? And for the record that's ERN 0108-1878. The English translation should be the last document, if you're working with the hard copy, the last document in this tab, which is PO2352G. Sir, do you recognise what's on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: It is a transcript or rather an intercept that had been recorded and noted down into the notebook by me. I listened it over on one of the UHER devices and noted it down into the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I just ask you, for the sake of the record, because there is a little bit of handwriting at the top of the document, your transcription begins with a line that has a couple of numbers on it, followed by -- by a couple of names. Can you just read those two lines into the record, please, sir, where your transcription begins?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: It begins with the 12th channel or 12 K at 1910. "Participants Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, Zlatar at the switchboard, Palma at the switchboard, and Nikolic." And at the top, the part above what I've just read, that is from another intercept. I just kept on writing into the same notebook. There are several intercepts in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may, sir, may we look at PO2352C? And the English translation of that document should be the first page within that tab, the very first document, which is PO2352A, for the record. Do you recognise what that is, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: This is a typed-out telegram which was sent to the unit by using communication links and encrypted. It says at the top the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and then the unit, it says top secret, the southern location, and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is the date, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: The 20th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could just show page 2 of this document. And in the packets this appears as the first page of the printout, since we placed the page bearing the actual intercept as the first page and then the page -- any page bearing a date later on. Now, again, sir, would you just please read into the record the first two lines of this printout?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: It says "Azimuth 45," meaning 45 degrees compared to our location. Therefore we were receiving the signal from the angle of 45 degrees. "Frequency 822 megahertz, channel 12, time 1910 hours, participants Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic - Zlatar - Palma - Nikolic." I've explained already that Zlatar and Palma are the switchboards.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you compare this transcription line by line to see if there were differences, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I compared them, and the punctuation is somewhat different, the commas and question marks, and there was a word that was skipped. It was - - it is missing in the typed version, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do any of those differences change the meaning of the text in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: It didn't change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in preparing for your testimony, did I also ask you to listen to a CD recording of a conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I've listened to the recording from the CD.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as you listened to the recording, did I ask you to try to simultaneously read your handwritten transcription and compare that handwritten transcription to what you were hearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I compared it with my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber, sir, whether or not you were able to identify the conversation that you were hearing on -- from the CD as the one which you intercepted and transcribed, which we've been discussing here at tab 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes. This is the conversation. The change is that the introductory part was not noted down by me word for word when the two switchboards were communicating at the very outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll get to that in just a couple of seconds. In about a minute. If we could have PO235 -- actually, if we could queue up P02352D, please. And with the assistance of the usher I will put the transcript of this recording on the ELMO so we can see it. And the B/C/S transcript is at PO2352F, and that should be the second to last document in the packet or in the tab. And we can play that any time we're ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, without going into any specifics, were there any differences between what you heard on the CD and what you wrote in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: In essence the two are the same. They are identical. I couldn't follow the other part on the paper because it's not on the ELMO. Perhaps we could do that. We heard the whole recording, but the rest of the page could not be visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you are referring to the English translation, sir, being shown?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: No, the -- the Bosnian version. I couldn't follow it on hard copy because they didn't turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Based on your prior review, sir, and this will be my last question. Based on your prior review in listening to the CD audio tape, do you recall whether any of the differences that you noticed between what you heard and what you wrote changed the meaning of the intercept at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Nothing was changed in the essence. Maybe a few words are different, but the context is the same. It's the same conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer. As I take it, the Popovic team would like to cross-examine? Go ahead, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've listened carefully to the summary read out by my learned friend Mr. Thayer. Inter alia you confirmed that you received empty notebooks from the command and you were to use them to note down intercepts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition, you said that there was a registration or a file number in those notebooks together with the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, the so-called protocol. A filing number, because each notebook had to have its own number within the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "a unit," do you mean the company or the platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: The company.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that that date did not necessarily have to correspond to the dates of intercepts noted in the particular notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: The notebooks had been brought before, we would always get them before each shift. There were several notebooks, and we were on the top of the mountain, so this is how they delivered them to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are not allowing a pause between question and answer, both of you. So if I could please emphasise with you the need to pause between question and answer, because otherwise the interpreter will encounter great difficulties. All right? The reason is you speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, I will bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify something. The date on which you would start using a particular notebook would, as a rule, come after the date when that particular notebook was registered in your company. To give you an example, if the protocol number was the 1st of May, you would start using that notebook after the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it should be like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say it should be like that, does it mean that there were exceptions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Well, I didn't check all the dates in all the notebooks. It was not my job to do that, to see which date it was filed on. It was done by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you received all of them from the command, and they should have been filed with the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm saying that I wasn't the one to do that. Of course the first intercept in a given notebook should follow the date of the notebook's filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I don't expect my voice to remain a voice in the wilderness unheeded. It's barely one minute ago, and you've started doing exactly the same thing again. So please allow a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Court. Could we please show Exhibit from the 65 ter list bearing the number 2355 to the witness? Page 3, please. I apologise. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at the date? Is that the protocol date you mentioned alongside the number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it used to look like, but I should really have a look at the notebook. However, this does reflect the protocol number and the date as they used to look like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have nothing against you viewing the entire notebook, although I believe this copy should be authentic. Do you want to see the original?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I don't know which notebook this is, but this is what it used to look like. The protocol sign contained the number and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the original of that notebook, if possible? Is it the same number and date as on the copy you have before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the next page in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, can we place it on the ELMO, please? It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that the first date at the beginning of the notebook, the first intercept, is the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know who put that date there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I see the date, but whether it really corresponds to this intercept, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a look at page 2352B. It is the 37th page in the original, but we can also have a copy shown. It is 2352B from the Prosecutor's list. It was shown a little while ago during the examination-in-chief. If you go to page 37 of the notebook, you should find this particular intercept that you've seen a few minutes ago. Can we agree that there is no date here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: If I may have a moment to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please be my guest.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, this is a copy from the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and you gave your answers concerning this intercept when my learned friend Mr. Thayer was questioning you. Since we see no date there, how do you know what date it is? How did you know? Did you try to consult the other dates from the notebook, or did you follow the typed report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I went along the -- what I could see at the typed report, but maybe I can check that against my own handwriting. There doesn't seem to be a date. Therefore, I probably concluded what the date was from the typed-out report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something else. Can you tell me how many notebooks were in use simultaneously while you were on duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I don't know how many exactly. We would use several notebooks. One would be sent to the typist, and in the meantime I would use another one. Therefore, the typist would have one notebook, and I would have another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We heard some other intercept operators testifying here and they told us that they would use the same notebook until they would reach their end. In other words, they would say there were several workstations, four workstations manned by two operators at the same time, each one would follow two devices, and that each one of them would have a separate handbook and when there would be a change of shift, after the two hours, that person would continue writing down into the same notebook. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: To be specific, I would take the notebook which was there, which was in use, and I would simply continue writing. While the typist had one notebook, I would have another. I don't know how many were in use simultaneously at any given time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While working on those intercepts how many operators were there together with you at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: There were two persons in each shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And each one of you had one notebook, I presume?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: We had several notebooks. We could have several.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that he could write in whichever one he wanted at that moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: The ones which had been used previously, or if they were complete, full, then we could start a new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, is it possible that there may have been as many as seven notebooks used at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My next question is this: So on any given day one could use the notebook number three, then the notebook number two, then the notebook number one and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: One could use the notebooks that were there physically, present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that you have noted something that I had, because you mentioned it in your testimony, that there are dates missing in many notebooks. For example, you identified as many as nine of your intercepts bearing no date. Can you tell me how one can determine what the exact date was if one was to use only the notebook? Is it possible at all if you had, say, seven notebooks used at the same time, it could mean on the 13th you entered one conversation, and then you used some other notebooks, then on the 16th you returned to the original one where you noted down the conversation of the 13th, and you just continue writing down conversations without any dates. In other words, if one was to go through that notebook, could naturally presume that the second conversation was noted down on the 13th where the first one was, since it bore no date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: It wasn't our practice that we would note down dates. Sometimes I put the dates in, sometimes I didn't. In the same room where we were, there was the computer used by the typist, and I would simply give him the notebook right away and he would start typing. In the computer, there were templates with the azimuth, the frequency, the channel, depending on which was used. That's where we would put in dates. Therefore, there was no need for us to put them into the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You remember your initial testimony before this Tribunal probably, and I can try and jog your memory as well. On that occasion you said that in the shift there were technicians, people who were tasked with operating antennae?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: You mean special people who worked with the antennas. Yes. We knew who was entrusted with the antennas. That was allocated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was also a person who took care of the tape recorder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Well, we all took care of the tapes, but it was actually his task to put them altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there was a person in charge of the tape recorders, you mean for -- the person in charge of collecting all the tapes? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, other than the duty of section commander, did you perform any other duties in this platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I had duty shifts in the kitchen. I don't know whether that was in that period in July, but we had to cook for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's take this time before you were sent to Sarajevo for training. Until the 1st of May, 1995 did you carry out any other duties other than being the section commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one moment, please. Excuse me. While you were training in Sarajevo did you know that the command of your unit requested that you be promoted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please look at Exhibit 2D50?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to be on the safe side, Your Honour, if this -- this document will not be broadcast? I just want to get some confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usually the instructions so far, and I understand they are being adhered to, are not being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There may be some biographical information, so I just caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe we will go into private session, maybe that is wiser. Mr. Zivanovic, shall we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. To the Beara team, I understand, no cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, we have no questions. We are passing our time to the rest of the Defence teams, under your order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. When is Mr. Ostojic back?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I spoke to Mr. Ostojic yesterday, there are some personal problems, family problems that have arisen. He should be back on Monday of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Nikolic will be next. What happened to Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon will be away for two or three days. He is on duty at his office, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Nikolic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You testified today on page 11 of the transcript, lines 15 to 18 that when you did not hear a conversation from the beginning and you did not transcribe it from the beginning, you would place three dots at the beginning indicating this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Not every time, but in most cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of January when you were preparing to testify before this Tribunal, besides listening to the audio material, which was played in the courtroom today, you were also shown the transcript of this conversation, the transcript was drafted by the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, I was shown the transcript by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you read it carefully; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I assume that you compared it to the handwritten version from notebook 220, which was shown to you a number of times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You noticed some differences between those two texts; is that correct? From the text which is the transcript of the Prosecution of the conversation and the handwriting version in notebook 220?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, there are some differences.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the Witness Exhibit P2352B and F? These are B/C/S versions of this document that the witness and I discussed. For those who will be following in English, it is also Exhibit 2352, the translation is E, and the handwritten version is G. And can we have them all on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We cannot have all of them on the screen. One by one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We can have on the ELMO hard copies if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if this is easier on the ELMO, then I would prefer that, and it will be also easier for the witness to follow the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before we put the text on the ELMO, sir, could you please tell me, in terms of these two texts, when you saw them again and when you heard the cassette again, you would agree with me that the text by the Prosecution is much closer to the actual conversation on the audiotape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes. It's more precise conversation, but the context of the conversation is the same. What was important to us was the information, the actual context, but we didn't really bother much with the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But from what I understood, there are differences in some words between the Prosecution's transcript and your notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And the transcript of the Prosecution resembles much more closely the original version. Could we please look at two versions on the ELMO for the witness to see, or if that's not possible, we can look at them one by one. I really wanted to cut this short. Can we show the Witness 2352B and 2352F? For those who are following it in English, it's 2352G and 2352E.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, could the counsel please say the ERN number, since we don't have the 65 ter number in the hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course: 0108-1878. 0822. That is the F. Just one second. The same number is on the English and the B/C/S version. 0822. So this can be confusing, but perhaps we can put the B/C/S version of the transcript up. 0822 B/C/S transcript. I've got the 65 ter numbers which were furnished to us by the Prosecution. Yes. Yes, that is the B/C/S version of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the beginning of this conversation in the notebook? Your notebook, and that would be the ERN number 0108-708. 0108-1878. If I'm not mistaken that would be page 36 of the notebook. Is that correct, sir? Are these the two documents that we would like to look at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, I found it in the notebook, and also I found the transcript done by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My question to you, please help me understand, we have the participants up here on the transcript if you look at the screen N, Nikolic; Z, Zlatar; P, Lieutenant-Colonel, and then the name, and then the text begins. In your notebook, if we leave out the azimuth, the channel and the time, there is one more word, and that is "Palma," and that is not on the transcript of the Prosecution and we agreed that the transcript faithfully conveys what is on the audiotape that we heard in the courtroom today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: The conversation that we looked at, you could not hear the Palma switchboard, I think. You could not hear it. I wrote that before.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You wrote that much earlier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: The procedure when I'm recording a conversation, while the device is scanning, it is sweeping the memorised channels, memorised in the device, and then when it comes to the 12th channel the device is stopped, I can already hear the conversation in my headphones, and then I press the record button. So it's not right from the beginning. This would happen in the interval. You could hear the Palma switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you assumed that because today you don't hear that in the recording?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: No, you don't hear that on the audiotape.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's not there. You don't hear it. So today we assume that that word at the time could have been Palma?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I wrote it for me on a piece of paper. I had a plain piece of paper in front of me, and I would write down the time, the frequency, the channel where the participant was talking and then I would just note down briefly who participated in the conversation because then I could go back to the actual conversation. We would be taping several conversations at the same time, so I would have notes on the paper so that I could refer back to the actual conversation when I was listening back to it. I wouldn't immediately listen back to a conversation once it was over. I wouldn't immediately begin to transcribe these conversations.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you see that piece of paper when you were preparing for today's testimony? Does that paper exist today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: No, I mean it was just an internal thing so that I could later transcribe the proper conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Therefore, today from the audio recording we have and the transcripts made from that and based on everything you heard here today, we cannot say for certain that the word "Palma" was uttered, Palma being an designator of one VRS unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: You cannot hear it on the tape, but I know what I heard and I noted it down on a piece of paper. That was the procedure that was in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please refer to the notebook before you, the original. It is Exhibit P2355. For e-court it is 0108-1875. Three or four pages after this. 0108-1875. You will see that number in the upper right-hand corner in the notebook. Maybe it will assist you, and I believe this is where we begin with your handwriting. It says 11822 towards the bottom of the page. So 11, then 822000.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You marked the channel, the frequency, and the time, and participants 1 and 2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It means that you didn't identify the participants in this particular conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please go to the next page, the last four -- three digits are 876. We have the eighth channel at 1845?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please read out the collocutors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: The duty officer lieutenant Simic, and Palma, Captain Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And Matkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What follows is the actual conversation transcribed by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did not find any of the names mentioned in the first line. You start using K and M from line 4 onwards. What was the basis for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I'm telling you the introductory part, whereby they introduced themselves, I did not transcribe that. I would note down their names and I know who it was. Therefore, I had it on a piece of paper and it should probably be on the tape, the entire conversation. I would have to listen to the entire conversation and based on the recorded conversation, I could respond to your question whether they introduced themselves or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So merely going through the text written by you wouldn't mean much in this instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Well, I didn't write that down for nothing or out of the blue. Either they were mentioned on the tape or I heard them introduce themselves. But that introduction, the greetings and formalities, I didn't note those things down.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If we are to believe that the participants are as designated here, not a single name begins with the letter K. Therefore, it is possible that there was another participant who was not mentioned. Someone whose name begins with a K?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, there is a captain, K means captain, and in this case it is Milosevic. K, captain. We have Matkovic and Milosevic. And we cannot have two collocutors with the same initial or with the same letter used throughout, so this K should be Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let us go to the next page, 1877. These are the last four digits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, Matkovic or Milosevic? K stands for Matkovic or for Milosevic? Because when he said K stands for captain, I got the impression that he was referring to Captain Milosevic. Was he referring to Captain Milosevic or to Captain Matkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] K is Captain Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the next page it begins with 19 K and 1900. Could you please read out the names of participants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Colonel Andric, Brana, that was the name for the switchboard, and Zlatar, Palma, and Captain Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They also did not introduce themselves in this text, it is the same case as the previous intercept. You did not put the three dots that you usually put?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: It's not there, but it should be on the recording or on the piece of paper where I initially noted it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the recording is the more authentic one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: It should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And if there is something missing on the tape, it means it wasn't said; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Well, I wrote things down on a piece of paper. I don't know what I wrote down in this particular case. And I don't know what originally came from the tape. I cannot hear it now so as to be able to tell you whether it came from the tape or from the paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I understand you. But in both my questions in both of these intercepts you said if I were given the recording I could tell you. Therefore I'm asking you whether the recording is the most authentic recording or transcription of a given intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about this particular case. This was a long time ago, I listened to many intercepts, and I'm explaining to you the practice that was in place. I would note down the collocutors who may or may not have introduced themselves. But as to whether it is on the actual recording, well, I don't know. Sometimes we would start recording a bit later. I could hear something in my headset, but by the time I've pressed a button, it may be gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But without a switchboard designation, you cannot say for sure who the collocutors are and where they come from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Without the specific switchboard designator --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Popovic, are you all right? If you are not all right, please tell us. THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was promised that I would be examined by a physician during the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Weren't you examined before the sitting? Before we started? THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] They couldn't locate the doctor, the physician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let's stop here and give him the opportunity. I was watching him, he is obviously having problems with his eyes. Let's have a 20-minute break, if we need to prolong it until he's seen by the doctor, we will do so. You will keep us informed. I'm sorry for interrupting you like this, Madam Nikolic, but in any event it is time for the break, okay. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, I have been informed by Madam Registrar about the developments. I have, after discussing with the other judges given instructions -- it's okay, you can remain seated. I've given instructions to locate the doctor as early as possible and get him here to visit you. In the meantime, if you are feeling uncomfortable following the proceedings, do let us know and we can let you sit somewhere else where you don't have all this light on your eyes and whatever. So, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We managed to move a mountain. Mr. Popovic, the doctor is now available and he can see you. So I don't know what the procedure is for security to escort him downstairs to the clinic. In the meantime, I take it that we can continue, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have only a few questions left. We left off when we were discussing participants and switchboards. I wanted to ask you this: When you have no switchboard noted down, we don't know where the collocutors are calling from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: One could know that because of the channels used, the channels they regularly used. I don't know in which specific cases that could have been done, but certain switchboards always used certain channels.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But we couldn't establish that as a rule?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't always like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will have but a few questions for you for the sake of clarification. Today on several occasions you mentioned that when listening in to the conversations, you would note down the beginning on a certain piece of paper. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I said that I used a piece of paper to note down the participants as well as the channel and frequency, or the number that was on the UHER recorder, something that would jog my memory, something that I could immediately link to a specific conversation. If they discussed ammunition I would note down "ammo."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with those pieces of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: We would usually throw it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: A part of the conversation, that part written down on that piece of paper, would that be transferred into the notebook or would none of it be transferred into the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: We would put in the channel, time, and frequency, as well as the participants. We would transfer that into the notebook, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why then write it down on a piece of paper first and then put it into a notebook?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been gone over by this witness already in this session, or the previous session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection upheld. Next question, or rephrase the question if you are eliciting some other kind of information, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The things you wrote down on those pieces of paper, would you do that simultaneously while listening to the conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I think that was clear from his prior answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, please try to review or revisit areas of the testimony that he himself, let alone others, that he himself has already testified about. You've got 15 minutes, try to concentrate on what is really fundamental for your client, if there is anything fundamental for your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I did not wish to repeat myself, I just wanted to clarify a couple of things. I will try and rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you noted things down into notebooks would you write it down simultaneously while listing to what had been recorded, or would you use the portion written down on that piece of paper as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Asked and answered. I'm reluctant to further the delay by objecting, but it's been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is one slight aspect to it that maybe has not been answered, but let's proceed. Answer the question, I think it will come to the end quicker that way. Go ahead. Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think your microphone is switched off. And could you repeat what you said, please, because the interpreters couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the question. Concerning the piece of paper, a part of that information would be entered into the notebook. Several conversations would be recorded, one after another, and I would note down information about those conversations on a piece of paper. And then I would rewind the tape and listen, or rather relisten to the conversations. Then I would decide on what information would be taken down into the notebook and what would not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's enough. Next question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next thing I wanted to ask you is this: Please focus on what you have before you, on what you have in the notebook. In the text you have in front of you, you wrote the channel and the time; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The channel and the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the typed version of the same text, we have the azimuth and frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what information would the typist write down the azimuth and the frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I would write down the frequency while listening to the conversation. I was working with the RRU-800, and at the beginning on this page here, you could see the frequency, the channel and the time. And all the conversations were on the same frequency. The azimuth was already -- or had been typed into the computer. We had templates. And then we would simply copy it, depending on the number of conversations, with this particular frequency, 822 megahertz, and then we would have 45 and the channel, or rather we would put in the channel, the time and the collocutors subsequently. The frequency had already been entered, as well as the channel, perhaps, and then we would transfer data from the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To conclude, there are discrepancies or differences between what was written into the notebooks and the typed versions. Which of the two is more authentic, more correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Linguistically speaking, the typed version, the computer version. Grammatically it is more correct; I have no commas, I have only a few question marks or dots, full stops.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Which of the two texts would reflect the actual conversation more accurately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: The typed version. The computer one. But to repeat, grammatically speaking, it would be more correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You're missing the thrust of my question. Which of the two texts would be closer to the original, to the actual conversation that had been intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: The one in the computer was more authentic because of the commas and so on. But he basically typed out what I had written. They're both -- I mean there are shades, nuances of difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you believe that the typewritten text is more authentic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Again, I say it's grammatically more correct, but as far as I'm concerned the one that I wrote down by hand is more authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Stojanovic. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Would it be possible to go to -- would it be possible to go in closed session to quote the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, yes. Go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, in this case a question was asked from you to know how the persons who were speaking and you were listening to could know that their conversation was being intercepted, and you answered: "[In English] They could hear it on the radio, and the standard procedure in the JNA was to take it as granted that the enemy was listening in. This was always a standard warning issued to everyone, 'the enemy is listening'." [Interpretation] Sir, did I understand you rightly that indeed the persons of the Republika Srpska army of which you were listening to knew that they were being listened to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: This had to do with General Mladic in 1992, I think. He was recorded, a conversation of his. Actually not one, but several were recorded where he was ordering something about live bait, or live meat. So they played that over the civilian radio station. This was a recording of that conversation of his, which I think was absurd to play a recording like that on the air waves, but it was their decisions, it wasn't up to me. As for "the enemy is listening," that was standard procedure, and it was written on every phone, on every telephone, "the enemy is listening."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My question -- my question was to know whether those who were being listened could know that they were being listened to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I don't know that. You would have to ask them if they knew or did not know that we were listening.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that your unit and the south site also should be on -- should try and jam the conversations, besides listening in to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Depends on the range. And it depends on the equipment that it was supposed to be blocking or interfering with. There were some hand-held radio stations and things. We also had a device for interference, it was called Kobac Holk [phoen] and it was a receiver -- a transmitter that could be operated from a helicopter and it operated on the RRU-1 range, so from 235 to 270 megahertz, it could interfere with the equipment. We didn't have such devices for an RRU-800 that could interfere with signals from that kind of device.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were these people in charge of jamming the conversations on RRU-1 were in the same unit as yours? They belonged to the same unit, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same unit. But it was just the interference section, they were named differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The commander was also their commander, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: They were attached. The platoon commander was the one from the electronic surveillance, but I don't know whether the section for interference was a section or a sector or a platoon. But it was together with us, together with the electronic surveillance department in the same section. As for the command, I don't know if the platoon commander was also the commander of that section or not. I am not sure who was commanding the interference unit when they were part of our section.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that a person in your squad was in charge of coding, encoding and encrypting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes. There was a person for encryption of telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How many members of your team could encrypt telegrams?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but there were plenty. Each shift at the facility had the encryption person and then we also had a person from another unit from the communication centre. It was a person who also worked on encryption.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that the chief of the squad had the power, the possibility to encrypt telegrams?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I don't know about him specifically. He had oversight of that. We couldn't print all the documents because there was a shortage of printing paper, so we were not able to do that. And he had to work on this using the computer. He would have to look at anything that came in on the computer, I was also signed in as an encryption person so that I would also be able to read the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did I understand you, you and your commander, your direct chief or commander, could access directly to the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes. We could use the computer. Which was also used for the crypto-protection work.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know if the person who sent the reports containing the intercepts also sent the reports concerning the jamming of conversations concerning some intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not informed about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D158?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report of November 1994, and I would like you to enlighten me on two points. First of all you have in front of you an intercept, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I really cannot see. This is not sharp enough on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could this be blown up a bit? May it be enlarged a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Could I please have the hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, could you have a look at this paper, but please confirm it. I'm just asking you if it was an intercept, I'm not asking you to comment upon it or to analyse it. Just tell me if it is an intercept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes. This is an intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if you look at the bottom of the page, there is a note concerning the jamming of conversations. Is that true? On the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, it says, "Remark." This is the radio station frequency, a hand-held radio station. It could also be a stationary one, but that could apply to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could the top of the document be shown? Sir, can you see the rectangular seal at the top of the document? I would like to know if you had an opportunity to see such stamps on documents when you were in your unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know who used to put this stamp on the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'm not sure, 100 per cent. I think this was done by the encryption operator.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, this seal would have been stamped there by the person who was sending the report or the person who received the report on site?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he just testified he wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sustained. Move to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell me, and this is my last question, to whom you sent or to whom the operator who encrypted would send the report, the operator who was encrypting, to whom did he send this report, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-123
utterances.text: I cannot see from what is here whom he would --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, my question was of a general nature. Answer only if you know. Do you know to whom the report of your unit was being sent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That question is of such a general nature that I'm not sure that it can be answered in the way it's been asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but if he knows, he can answer it. If he don't know, he won't answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The encryption operator knew to whom the radio reports were supposed to be sent. This radio report -- well, there was analysis section in the unit, I don't know if he took it first to the company commander or if he directly handed it over to the section that analysed the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it that the other Defence teams do not wish to cross-examine the witness? Mr. Haynes, what about Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa is been delayed on his way back from Belgrade, he's been sick the last week or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I asked you just for the record, if for no other reason. Is there any re-examination, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. There are no further questions for you, sir, which means that your testimony ends here. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence and on behalf of everyone here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go through the document-tendering process. There is a Prosecution list, descriptive list, which has been communicated to you, I suppose? Yes, I note Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to Exhibit 2352C. Or rather D. 2352D, which is the audiotape. First of all, it's not a tape, it's either a CD or a DVD, and even more important, we don't know whether it's the original or a copy, and if it is a copy, a copy of what? What is the original material that the copy is derived from, who made it and when? And for these reasons we object about this being admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Any further comments from the Defence teams? I hear none. Mr. Thayer, would you please address the two points or three points raised by Mr. Popovic -- Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. Again, this is a CD recording that has been made from a reel-to-reel tape which is contained -- I believe which contains previously admitted conversations which have been played in this courtroom. Again, had there been a request, we would have informed Defence counsel of that specific information. But that is the providence of the recording that was played today. The Defence has been furnished with the CD copy of the very recording that was played in court today and it is again based on a reel-to-reel tape which is in our evidence locker, Your Honour, in the vault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it's not enough, what the Prosecutor believes, that he believes that as copy of the original tape. That is not sufficient to have this admitted into evidence. We would need to have some reliable proof to know what exactly this is, when the copy was made, by whom, and from what. Was it a copy of a copy or a copy from the original. This is the sort of information we would need to have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, there's been previous testimony through a witness whose name I won't mention, that described the process of certain tape-recorded materials being furnished to the Office of the Prosecutor. In addition, the witness authenticated the recording himself as being what he heard. Now, whether -- what was played in the courtroom was a CD made of a tape -- a reel-to-reel tape, you know, that's something that can be argued at a later date in terms of the authenticity. But this witness authenticated the tape, he listened to it before, he listened to it in the courtroom, and he identified that as the conversation he listened to. We've already had previous testimony describing the process by which the tapes were furnished to this office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there are two things here my learned friend, Mr. Thayer, is mixing up. One thing is that the witness said this is a conversation identical to the one he noted down but he didn't say that was the actual conversation he recorded. Obviously the conversation was recorded on a reel-to-reel recorder, and this is not what was played here. The witness did not provide any information about the rerecording of the conversation, who, when, whether it's from the original tape or from some other media. I think we would need to clarify these two things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your final comment, Mr. Thayer, do you have any? The witness that had come over and testified about the handing of material from -- from BiH, ministry of justice or home affairs, et cetera, did that information cover this audiotape as well or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I believe it did, Your Honour. And if upon review of the record it didn't, we can certainly present that information later, but that is my understanding. That this -- this conversation was included along with at least two other conversations which have been played in this courtroom on the same reel to reel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And the other thing is that the conversion from reel to reel to CD format was done here at the office of the Prosecution, or way back in BiH?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That was done here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you can provide information as to who did it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I suppose this would be logged in your records?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can't vouch for every step of the recording. I presume at some level there is a notation that the evidence was taken out of the vault, for example, and something was done with it, but I can't represent that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And if there is a request by any of the Defence teams, significantly from Mr. Zivanovic, to have the original reel to reel that came into your possession a time back, would it be possible for you to make it available?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely. That has been a standing offer for a couple of months now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any further objections on any of the other documents that the Prosecution seeks to tender? All right. So first two are admitted under seal. Rest, please refer to the Prosecution document, what's involved goes under seal. Intercepts are marked for identification purposes, same as regards the notebook. Let me consult my colleagues on the audiotape and we will tell you exactly what's the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our decision on the audiotape is that it will be received for the time being marked for identification. And that's because it forms part of the general objection that there is from the Defence teams in relation to the authenticity of the entire process of intercepting and transcribing the intercepts. So then Mr. Zivanovic, you have two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we did furnish a list of the documents that were used in the cross-examination, and it's with the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... first one, BiH proposal for promotion, did you make use of it with the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The first exhibit is 1D157 and the second one is 2D50, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 2D50 that I'm referring you to. Okay. So these two documents are admitted marked for identification for the time being pending translation, unless there is an objection, a substantive objection on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hear none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, both under seal. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, 5D. Can you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D158.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has this been translated? I don't think so, that's why I am asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, but I'll let you know as soon as a translation is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So it will have the same fate as the previous documents, it will be marked for identification and automatically promoted then once we have a confirmation of a translation which is accepted. All right. Mr. Zivanovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I also used the 2355, the Prosecutor's intercept book. I don't think that the entire notebook was tendered into evidence by the Prosecutor, so I would just like to add that I used that one page with the date when the notebook was registered, that was entered on that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Madam Registrar, do you think you can locate, identify the page that -- from the transcript that was made use of.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is my understanding that Prosecution tendered the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That solves the problem; in other words, we don't have a problem. I am advised that since the next witness has been granted the protective measures of voice distortion, we need to stop the sitting for about 10 minutes, 10 to 15 minutes. Five to 10 minutes so they make the necessary installation of the special microphone. As soon as they are ready, we will -- I don't think we're going downstairs, we will stay here. --- Break taken at 4.53 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems that someone has decided that we don't understand your English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've heard that before. I've -- during the break, I spoke with the Popovic team and they have confirmed that we can go ahead, even though it is a new witness now, that that's not a problem and there is one matter I wanted to raise in private session, it will take two seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
