utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence, and our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration to the effect that your testimony will be truthful, that you will be testifying the truth in other words. Madam usher is handing you the text now, please read it out and that will be your commitment to this Tribunal that you will testify the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a seat, and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In order to make you feel more relaxed while you're giving evidence, we have granted you some protective measures, which I hope are to your satisfaction. I understand they have already been explained to you. One is we will not refer to you by name, we will use a pseudonym, and then your face and your voice will be distorted. In other words, I suppose this has been explained to you. What I want to know is whether this is to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nicholls will be examining you now, and then he will be followed by cross-examinations from the various Defence teams. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I start by showing the witness and my colleagues the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, could you please read the pseudonym sheet. Please don't read it out, could you just confirm yes or no, is that your name written on the sheet?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That will be PO2357 under seal, if it could be shown to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to try and go through this quite rapidly. I have a short direct examination. As we talked about earlier, please try to keep your answers concise, if you can. First, in your own language in my office, did you read your May 1999 ICTY statement, the entire statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you attest that that statement accurately reflects what you stated during the taking of this statement, that that information that is there is accurately recorded?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you also attest that your answers would be the same today if you were asked the same questions that formed the basis for that statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will now read a brief summary of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The witness was born in 1966. He is a Muslim by faith. As a teenager, he earned a diploma in electronic communications. The witness joined the ABiH army in September 1992. And in October, he joined the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit or PEB of the 2nd Corps. He became a squad commander in this unit and remained so until April 1993, at which time he was transferred elsewhere to work on a system related to Morse code messages. At the end of 1993, the witness was assigned to actively monitor VRS command lines of communications. And this was at what we have referred to as the southern location. From the spring of 1994, the witness was assigned elsewhere, and returned to his monitoring duties now at the northern location, in the spring of 1995. The process described by the witness in his statement of recording and transcribing intercepts at the northern location is similar or identical to the process we've heard many times. From June or early July 1995, the witness worked at this northern location as a signals communicator. He would encrypt intercepts and send them to the higher command. However, during this time, he also continued to monitor and transcribe intercepts as necessary. The witness was shown a notebook from this location and recognised his handwriting on several pages of the intercepts. The witness listened to an audiotaped conversation between General Krstic and Major Obrenovic which he recognised as a conversation that he had intercepted and transcribed in notebook 106. The witness left the ABiH in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to ask you a few questions about the review of intercepts that we did together in my office. Do you recall reviewing 15 handwritten intercepts in my office on a blue binder, such as the one I'm holding up, with tabs?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You recognise your handwriting on each written intercept in that binder?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You also reviewed the original notebooks which contained these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You recognise your handwriting as well for each of the intercepts in the packet in the corresponding original notebooks?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you confirm to the Court that you recorded and transcribed all of the 15 intercepts contained in the packet?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you just a couple questions about your work as an encryptor. From June-July of 1995 you worked at the northern location. The question is, when an intercept operator gave you a -- an intercept in a notebook to type up, encrypt and send off, did you ever make changes in the -- from the notebook to the final printout?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: For the most part, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On the occasions when changes were made, why were they made and how did that come up, if you can answer briefly?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: In case I would notice something that would strike me as illogical in the handwritten text, I would consult the operator, who had taken it down from the tape, and we would work on it together. Sometimes we would involve other people as well, if need be, and we would go back and relisten to the given intercept so as to be able to establish whether there was a mistake made. If we found one, we would make the necessary changes in the printed version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to show you an intercept and ask you a couple questions about it. This is the intercept at tab 13, 65 ter number 0993, and if I could have B up on the screen, which is the handwritten version. If we could also have the translation, which I believe is A. And scroll down to the bottom, please. Now, we see the names in brackets next to X and Y, and I'm referring to where it says General Krstic and Borovcanin of the specials. Can you tell me what the brackets mean when we see the brackets in one of your intercepts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. You left your microphone on, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, I think you need to go back to the moment he started answering this question. All right? And no transmission. Please be careful, because I mean we have to concentrate on many things, an extra one is always an extra. So...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So based on the beginning of the conversation, we would decide whether to tape it or not. What would happen usually was that we wouldn't know who the collocutors were, and then we would mark them as the person X and Y. Later on, if we learned of their identity during the conversation, then we would subsequently add their names in the brackets. We would write down -- designate which is collocutor X and the collocutor Y.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. In this intercept in line 2, it states, "Hello, this is Borovcanin, General, how are you?" And at the top of the intercept, in the parenthetical, you have written "Borovcanin from the specials." Can you tell us why you wrote that, "from the specials," after Borovcanin's name at the top?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Most likely I heard that on the device, I heard him introduce himself. But that part had not been recorded. That is why it is not in the transcribed portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could have the printout up, please, which is C. And I understand it will not be broadcast. Okay. I need to show a little bit more of the top, please. That's fine. Could I go into private session, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to now ask you a question about another intercept, this is the one at tab 15. And if I could have 1387B on the screen, please. And while that's coming up, sir, I can ask you, do you recall that I played you a CD recording of a conversation in my office?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you recognise that recording?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Excuse me. The text I see on the screen, well that's not the recording I had heard. It was another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, you're jumping ahead of me a little bit. If we could scroll down a little bit on the screen. And let me ask my question again. When I played you that recording, did you recognise the recording?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: The one I can see now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then just to be clear, the recording I played you, you recognised, was the same recording which you've transcribed here in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is, for the record, I said 1387B, but it is the intercept which begins on page 0080-4463 that took place at 9.50 and continues on the following page. I'm done with that. Can we go into private session now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 5.30. Earlier we had a mind stopping for 15 minutes' break after the Prosecution finished their examination-in-chief. But because of that microphone glitch, I need your advice. 20 minutes. All right. I think we can't do it otherwise. So we'll have a break of 20 minutes now. And then we will continue and proceed until 7.00 without a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, let's proceed. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, sir. Reading the statement you gave to the investigators, I saw that in 1994, the spring of 1994, you were transferred to the communications centre for anti-electronic warfare in the 2nd Corps. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: It's possible, I cannot remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement, it says that you received encrypted telexes from these other locations, such as this location where you went later and that you talked about later. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the accused Popovic is back in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were receiving these crypto-protected reports from these locations, did you have any kind of record of the reports that you received?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From 1995 onwards when you came here to testify, did you have an opportunity to see these records?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if the records were in a notebook or a book?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now please look at the following document: 1D156. Can you see that this is a document with the title protocol?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That it was sent by the encryption section from one of these locations, that it sent to the company, the encryption company of the 2nd Corps, there is a date there, but it's outside of the time that is relevant for the -- for us. Then there is an encoded name underneath of eight letters and numbers. There is a date and a time and then there is a greeting from the unit that is sending out the document. What I would like to know is whether you remember if such documents were drafted in the platoon that sent these documents or in the company that received the documents?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you worked at this facility, whose name I will not mention, from April 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I think it's May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You worked there also on listening in as well as a communications person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were intercepting the conversations, you were transcribing the conversations into a notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These were notebooks given to you by your unit's command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And before you received the notebooks, they were given a registration number and a date when these notebooks were registered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you gave your first statement to the Hague Tribunal investigators you told them what you wrote down in the notebooks, of course you remember that. I'm just going to remind you that you wrote down the usual things and what others also mentioned before; the frequency, the channel, the collocutors if you knew them, but you also said that you wrote down the tape number. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You cannot recall having said that?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I have probably said that, but since a lot of time has passed I cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just the usual, if he's going to be asked what he said to us and what is written down, it makes sense to give him a copy in his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. You are correct. If you are going to elaborate on this, please make the text available to the witness, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show D252 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, just -- this should not be broadcast, because it's got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Instructions, Mr. Nicholls, are that they are not broadcast unless we say so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D52. Page 3 of the B/C/S. Also page 3 of the English. Could we please have -- well, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 3, the penultimate paragraph. The third sentence of that paragraph. It reads: "I would note down the time, either based on my watch or the clock that was on the recorder. I would also note down the frequency, the channel and the tape number, since they all had numbers. The counter and participants, if it was possible to identify them." Do you recall it now?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I believe it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You had the opportunity to see the notebooks. You were shown them by the Prosecutor, not only here in the courtroom, but in his office as well; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in any of those notebooks, see the tape number?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see in any of the notebooks the state on the counter, the number on the counter?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to have a look at a document, and I have to tell you that it wasn't drafted by you; however, you are the first person to address encryption. The first witness that we have who worked on encrypting the intercepts, and you may be the last as well. Could you please explain, therefore, some of the principles in place, because the colleagues of yours whom we heard before you were not familiar with that portion of the work. It is Exhibit 1D93. As you can see, there is a correction. It wasn't sent from your facility, but from another one. First of all, in the heading you can see a number. It says, "Top secret," and then the number. Can you tell me whether that number was typed into the computer by the operator or was it a pre-programmed number automatically assigned to each of the documents in the computer?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, then. I presume you cannot recall anything about the date as well, you don't know whether it was typed in by hand or whether it was allocated by the computer itself?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: No, we typed in the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you go through the text on the correction, basically it is only one sentence long. Would you agree with me if I said that you can see there that by comparing the protocol numbers, the sender of the report, the person from the platoon, realised that the person who was supposed to receive it at the company did not receive one of the three report files which had been sent the day before on the 2nd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct if I say that that file had been sent the day before the 2nd of August, 1995, at 11.30?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 11.33.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that it was a file which was the first out of the three report files?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I presume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says, "Our first report file was not received." Then we have a TBTD28NB?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Finally, is it correct that in addition to this correction the sender resent the file which they believed had not been received?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Below the line there is a number, a figure. Having a look at the number, can you determine whether that was the file which had not been received by the company?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the text of the report there? If you do, you will see that it includes three conversations in one report. Could we please scroll down the text for the witness so that he could see what follows. This is the second conversation, and on the next page we have the third.

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude then, therefore, that these conversations, the last of which was at 10.00; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The one before was at 9.50. Could you please scroll up. The previous page. 9.50, the conversation below. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the one just above was at 9.30?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we conclude, therefore, that this was the first report file which had not been sent or rather there was no proof of reception of the report having been sent at 11.33?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see any other possibility there?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we conclude that the other two report files were indeed sent at 11.33?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These files should have had consecutive numbers. If the first one was 02, then what should have followed was 03 and 04, if I understood it well.

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We were told by the Prosecutor that yesterday you had a telephone conversation with another witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not have a telephone conversation with another witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I apologise. It was via the hotel extension. Yes, there was a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking you about this because in their notification, they told us that you inter alia discussed the meaning of these codes that we see on the screen, for example, the ones we've just discussed. We see the TBTD28NB code?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Witness, don't start giving your answer to the question until you see Mr. Zivanovic's microphone off. We are trying to protect your identity as much as we can, and that's one way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that letter from the Prosecutor, we were also told that the code as seen here means the following: The first two letters pertain to the sender of the file; is that correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We were also told that the following two letters pertained to the receiver; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: It is possible, but I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We were also told that the following two letters or digits pertained to the date. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I was wondering if a translation was - may be available for the last document used by my colleague, because we haven't found it, but this is, if I'm correct, the same document used in the first week of December, so I didn't know if we have one that I was missing or if it is not yet available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't help you. Maybe Mr. Zivanovic can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we used this document during the examination of another witness. I can mention his name in a private session because it's a protected name. That's when the translation was asked for. But we still don't have it. I don't know if the translation of that document has been completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The Beara team, Defence team. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, at this time we don't believe we have any questions. I believe Ms. Nikolic will cross-examine next, and after it's all said and done I may have questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to put just a few questions to you relating to one of the intercepts which you recognised from amongst the 15 that you were shown in the Prosecutor's office in preparation for this testimony. It's the intercept at tab 7. Could we please show the witness exhibit marked for identification 2358D, and in English 2358E. The English is the D version, and the B/C/S version is marked as D. So the witness should look at version D. Sir, could you please look at this report compiled at your location. Familiarise yourself with the text. And my question is: When you listened to this conversation and when you transcribed it, you did not hear the name of the switchboard or the collocutors on the tape?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I don't have it here. I probably did, because it's written down, but I really cannot recall this specific conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: During the conversation, one of the collocutors introduced himself, that's Jankovic, and that's when you introduced that name. The second collocutor did not introduce himself, so he remained as Y; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The name of the switchboard was not mentioned on the tape, otherwise you would have written it down, whether it was badem, bakar or whatever?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes, that is very probable.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If you don't have the name of the switchboard it's hard to know which unit the collocutors belonged to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: My assignment wasn't to know which unit the collocutors belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I agree, but now if we were reading it and wanted to establish from which unit the collocutors came from, we wouldn't be able to establish that, just like you were not able to establish that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Well, at this time I wouldn't be able to determine that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Probably if you had the tape you would be able to relisten to it and then see?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Maybe yes, and maybe no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me that the last name Nikolic is quite a common name in that area and that there were a lot of participants with that last name?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that just in the Drina Corps there were 272 soldiers and officers with this last name, you would agree with me, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Apparently I'm to go next, Your Honour. I'm quite happy to, I won't be very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness, it's right, isn't it, that the SDB operated at the same location, the one where you worked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, just for clarity to narrow that down, because there were several places he worked at I talked about in the summary and -- but it's up to my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'd better go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. That's what we'd better do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question now that we are back in open session. The question was: Did you do any encryption work for the SDB?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I really cannot remember. I don't think so though.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you have no recollection of making any corrections to any encryption work for the SDB that would, for example, be different to what you described when you were being asked questioned by my learned friend? In other words, the operation would have been the same for the SDB encryption as for your own, as far as you were concerned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think that's a fair question, given his last answer that he doesn't believe that he did so. I don't see how he can speculate whether he did, whether it would have been the same or different along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's rely on the witness first to see whether he can answer the question as it is. If he finds difficulties with it, then we will ask you to rephrase it. But in the meantime, if he is in a position to give us a reply to it, an answer to it, then he should do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember having any contacts with any transcripts or notes or records or files of the SDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that answers the question. And that completes my cross-examination, therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we go into private session for my questions, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you came back to the same location in 1995, were there any people in charge of scrambling or jamming telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the previous statement you made before the Prosecutor's office you said that when a telephone conversation that you recorded seemed to be insignificant or impersonal, you actually went back with a tape. Does this mean you reused the tape or would you first erase what had been recorded beforehand that seemed to be insignificant?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: What seemed insignificant or unimportant was recorded over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would it be possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt, but just for the clarity of the record and the transcript, we've got "telephone conversations" in there, which I don't think is what my colleague is asking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure you are 100 per cent right. Let's go around it can in an easy way because it is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies from the interpreter's booth.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I will ask the same question, because there is a mistake in the transcript, in the English version, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So, when you rewind to record a new conversation which seemed insignificant, was this conversation actually -- or the previous conversation erased or would you actually just rerecord on the same tape?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I don't understand the question all that well, but I will give you an answer, perhaps it's satisfactory. When we began to record a conversation and we would be recording it and listening to it at the same time. When we concluded that it was a private conversation that was unimportant, we would go back on the counter to the beginning of this unimportant conversation and then for the next conversation we would again begin recording. So then this first unimportant conversation would be recorded over, a new conversation would be recorded over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. You answered very clearly to my question. Now, in this case I would like to ask you would it have been possible that at any time the new conversation would have not been recorded correctly and that the two would overlap? The two conversations, that is.

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: The recorded material for the most part was usable. It could be utilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we for just a brief moment, move into private session? Because I would like to mention the reference of the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go -- we're already in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sir, in the case I just mentioned you declared, "[In English] I personally did not rely on recognising the voice but only the information which I heard or recorded on tape. In some cases with respect to recognition of the voice itself, I would ask assistance from a colleague, although I should like to mention once again that I personally avoided identification by relying on the voice." [Interpretation] Sir, in view of what you said beforehand, can we thus conclude that identification through voice recognition is never absolutely reliable?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand your answer. Could you clarify that? Say how it could be yes and no?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: If you were to hear the voice of your child calling, would you recognise their voice?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's not up to me to answer any questions, but I understand. Let's say that I understand what you mean, and I'm going to move on to another question. Can we show the witness Exhibit P1112A? 1112B, and the English version is 1112A. Can we show the conversation starting at 12.40, it's the second one on this page. Sir, do you recognise your handwriting on this document?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is this a conversation which you both recorded and transcribed and then sent to your superior command?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: This is a conversation I recorded, transcribed from the tape, but I cannot remember if I was the one who sent it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And today do you remember this particular conversation? Do you remember the specific moment at which you recorded it?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you do not know who were the interlocutors in this particular conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But, in any case, today you are sure that you heard clearly one of the interlocutors saying, "[Previous translation continues] [In English] ... trucks and buses and the water tanks should be sent to give them water and food. This morning we organise it here. We will give them everything. I talked with them and we will accept all of the civilians who want to -- to and they can stay. Those who don't want to can choose where they will go." [Interpretation] It is this that you recorded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And although you don't know exactly who the interlocutors were in this particular conversation, you are sure that there were two members of the army of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sir, since at some point in time you worked on encryption and protection, could you tell us who this report was sent to?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: The report -- well, all the reports were actually sent to the communications centre of the intelligence organ of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was this location, this unit's location in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: If you are thinking of the communications centre of the intelligence organ, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In your statement for the Prosecutor's office in May 1999, you say the responsibility for writing the date down was that of the person in charge of encrypting messages. Would you give any allowance for possible mistakes in the dates on these reports?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: There is the possibility of grave mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can we show the witness -- witness Exhibit 5D159. Could we show the witness the top part of the document. Sir, can you confirm that this is the report which was sent from the location you were stationed at in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is it correct that somebody corrected the handwritten date?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Actually, a correction: "A handwritten correction to the date."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sir, do you know or did you have an opportunity of seeing this square stamp or rectangular stamp on the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you say who placed this stamp on the document?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is it correct that all official reports bore this stamp?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sir, can you see the number right above the date starting 01/17595. We heard testimony here that number one was the number of a report that was sent one day, and that the numbers following actually represented the date at which the report was sent. Can you confirm the fact that the reports were marked in this particular way?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you know, you can't remember whether this was the regular procedure, but do you know the date at which a particular procedure would have been set up for the purpose of marking documents and reports?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: No. I can explain. When I began to work in crypto-protection, this was already set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You said earlier on that you didn't know whether these numbers were handwritten or directly typed, but would you allow the possibility for a human mistake as well as an IT mistake in that there might have been mistakes in these numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just don't know the value of these kind of open questions of, Can anybody make a mistake? when he's already said once mistakes can be made. I think that is for argument later that doesn't need to go to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead and answer the question, please. I mean it covers more than what you actually stated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text is a typed text. The one that I'm looking at. All of them were like that. Therefore, all the information was typed in by hand. I don't remember specifically in this example where the stamp bears the number of the telegram Q9Q17860A. I don't remember whether this would be automatically generated. There is that possibility. It could be automatically generated or by hand. But the text itself was done by hand. It's a text file. There was no kind of automatic data entry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned the number, I mean the number you just mentioned, and you said that it was typewritten. Does this mean at any point in time all of the reports would bear this number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can safely move to the next question, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To conclude this topic I would like to show the witness Exhibit 5D165.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: On this document I would like to ask you a brief question regarding the number above the date. Would you agree to say that there is an obvious mistake in this number?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I agree. I think this was a grave mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I still have a series of questions to ask the witness, and I would like us to move into private session for asking these questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have got eight minutes left. Who wishes to go next? Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, to be honest, I don't believe I will be able to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you finish one chapter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask a question before you ask, Mr. Lazarevic? Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It just disappeared. You said on previous document you said there is a grave mistake on the date. How did you know that? Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the computer's keyboard, the number 7 and the slash are on the same key, and the typist typing probably forgot to press the shift key as well as the other one when typing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think I will have to switch places with Mr. Stojanovic because the neck of this microphone is much longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening. First of all, for the sake of protection of your identity, when you see the red light go off, only then should you begin talking, so as to not jeopardise the protective measures in place. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, before you came here to testify, we heard a number of your colleagues who worked at both the northern and the southern location and they gave us a certain piece of information that I wanted to corroborate with you. They spoke about the fact that certain people whose conversations were intercepted were or could be recognised based on the features of their voice, the type of speech, the terminology they used, and once they would hear a conversation based on those characteristics, they developed an ability to identify such people. Did you come to possess such a quality as well?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: I did, but I never relied too much on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In any case, I wanted to ask you a follow-up question based on the previous one. In the situation in which you hear a voice for the first time, the voice itself cannot be the basis for identification of that person. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A few questions now generally speaking about certain intercepts. You worked and performed the same tasks beginning -- from the beginning of 1993 until the end of the war more or less; is that so?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During that period you had the opportunity to hear thousands of conversations probably, some of which you recorded and transcribed. Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: PW-134
utterances.text: Well, I can't say for sure, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Out of that great number of conversations, although the exact figure is not that important, should mean that it is difficult for you to remember a specific conversation. You do not have an independent recollection of a given conversation or rather to put it in a simpler wording, had you not been given a notebook with your handwriting, you probably would not have been able to recollect a specific conversation. But by viewing or reviewing the notebooks and seeing your handwriting, this is what made it possible for you to be able to say that you indeed listened to that conversation? [Previous translation continues] [In English] ... to start with another topic, this may be, perhaps, the best moment to stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, we will continue tomorrow in the afternoon. In the meantime, you are still a witness still testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I am afraid the answer was not recorded. He agreed with me, but it was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is important that between now and when you resume testifying you do not communicate with anyone about the matters you are giving evidence upon. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And could we have your answer to the previous question, to the last question that Mr. Lazarevic put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So have a nice evening, all of you, and we'll meet again tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of January, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.,
